Stead
sted
n. (place; the room or position of another; rendering Hebrew tachath, Greek huper and anti in the substitutionary sense)
From the Saxon stede, a place or station, cognate with the German Statt and with English steady, homestead, instead. The root idea is a standing-place; to act in another's stead is to stand where he stood.

Biblical Definition

Stead is one of the most doctrinally loaded small words in the Authorized Version, because it is the ordinary English for substitution. On Moriah, “Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son” (Genesis 22:13). The ram does not assist Isaac or set him an example; it takes his place on the wood, and Isaac walks down the mountain alive because something died where he would have died. That is the shape of the atonement in narrative form, three chapters before the word lamb has any theology attached to it. Genesis uses the same construction at the other end of a grief: God “hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew” (Genesis 4:25) — Seth stands in the room Abel left. Job uses it to demand real sympathy: “if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you” (Job 16:4), which is an exact statement of how cheap counsel is from a man who is not standing where the sufferer stands. And Paul uses it of the preacher's office: “we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). The ambassador does not speak for himself; he occupies his master's place and speaks his master's words.

Webster 1828 Definition

Place; the room or position of another. It is the Authorized Version's plain word for substitution — the ram in the stead of Isaac, the ambassador in Christ's stead — and it carries the atonement in a single syllable.

expand to see more

STEAD, n. sted. [Sax. stede, a place; G. statt.] Place; the room which another had or might have.

2. In composition, a farm or dwelling place; as homestead, farmstead.

3. To stand in stead, to be of use or great advantage.

4. INSTEAD, adv. In the place or room of; as, put this instead of that.

5. In Scripture, of one offered or standing in the room of another; as the ram offered in the stead of Isaac, Gen. 22.

Key Scripture

Genesis 22:13 — "And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son."

Genesis 4:25 — "And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew."

Job 16:4 — "I also could speak as ye do: if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you, and shake mine head at you."

2 Corinthians 5:20 — "Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God."

Modern Corruption

Substitution itself is under attack. Penal substitutionary atonement is charged with being unjust or worse, and stead is quietly emptied so that Christ becomes an example or a victim rather than a substitute.

expand to see more

The modern objection to penal substitution is that it is arbitrary at best and monstrous at worst — punishing an innocent for the guilty is called a moral scandal, and the doctrine is set aside in favour of theories in which the cross chiefly demonstrates love, exposes violence, or defeats hostile powers. Each of those contains something true and none of them is the centre. Scripture's own picture is the ram in the thicket: Isaac is bound, the knife is raised, and God provides a life to be taken in the stead of the life that was forfeit. The substitution is not an unwilling third party seized at random; it is the Son given by the Father and giving himself, one Person in two natures, competent to stand in the room of many because of who he is. The objection collapses once the substitute is recognized as God himself in our nature rather than a bystander.

The principle to recover is that the ambassadorial sense in 2 Corinthians 5:20 depends entirely on the sacrificial sense in Genesis 22:13. A preacher stands in Christ's stead in the pulpit only because Christ stood in the sinner's stead at the cross. Strip out the substitutionary atonement and the phrase in Christ's stead becomes a mere formality of office. Keep it, and every faithful sermon is a man occupying a place he did not earn, begging men to be reconciled by a death he did not die.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tachath means under, in the place of — the preposition of substitution. Greek anti is in exchange for; huper is on behalf of, and in sacrificial contexts, in the place of.

expand to see more

Hebrew tachath (H8478) — underneath, in the place of; the ram offered in the stead of Isaac.

Hebrew kopher (H3724) — a ransom, the price paid in another's room; from kaphar, to cover, atone.

Greek anti (G473) — over against, in exchange for; his life a ransom anti many.

Greek huper (G5228) — on behalf of, in the place of; Christ died huper the ungodly.

Greek presbeuo (G4243) — to be an ambassador; the office of standing in another's stead.

Usage

"Of the substitutionary sacrifice: offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son (Genesis 22:13)."

"Of a place filled after loss: hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel (Genesis 4:25)."

"Of the preacher's office: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20)."
